transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (NovaPay CTO), Priya Kapoor (NovaPay ML Eng), Liam O'Rourke (NovaPay PM)

Auto-generated summary (auto):
- Quick Hosted API demo covering chat and text generation basics: streaming, key parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and best-practice retry/backoff semantics.
- Customer interested in latency SLOs for payment confirmation flows and cost estimate for 10M tokens/month.
- Next steps: pricing doc, latency benchmark, prompt set from customer.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro \u0004 I'm Ethan, I'm the AE on this account and with me is Maya our SE, she'll run the demo. How are you all?
[00:06] Carlos (NovaPay): Good, thanks. We got about 45 minutes, wanted to see hosted flow first, mostly chat generation, and understand retries and latency for sync payments.
[00:12] Maya (Redwood): Great. Today we'll demo the Redwood Hosted API for chat/text basics \u0004 streaming responses, key params like temperature and max_tokens, and how to handle retries and rate limits. I may talk through a few console screens as well.
[00:21] Priya (NovaPay): Sounds good. We care about 300ms p95 for short confirmations and cost per 1k tokens.
[00:27] Maya: Noted. Quick agenda: 1) API request/response shape 2) streaming behavior 3) parameter tradeoffs 4) retries/backoff & idempotency 5) console + Optimize suggestions.
[00:35] Ethan: I'll drop the pricing sheet and hosted vs dedicated comparison after the call.
[00:39] Liam (NovaPay): Cool. Let's start.

[02:05] Maya: Ok, showing the quick example \u0004 POST /v1/chat/completions to Redwood API, body includes model, messages, and we set stream=true for SSE streaming. Example: { model: "redwood-open-chat-1", messages: [{role: "user", content: "Confirm payment for $12.50 to Merchant X"}], stream: true, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 60 } \u0004 typing in the console playground now.
[02:31] Carlos: When you stream, does Redwood send partial tokens as they are generated? How often are events flushed?
[02:37] Maya: Yes, the stream provides incremental deltas; flush frequency depends on model and internal batching. Typical flush is every few tokens or on sentence boundaries. For low-latency use cases you can tune chunking via the streaming client buffer, but server-side we optimize for throughput vs latency.
[02:55] Priya: Is there websocket support or SSE only?
[02:58] Maya: We support SSE for browser/HTTP streaming and gRPC/streaming API for server-to-server. The SDK also exposes a streaming helper that emits token events.

[04:10] Maya: Quick note on params \u0004 temperature controls randomness: 0.0 is deterministic. For confirmations you probably want 0.0\u00040.2. max_tokens caps output length; top_p is nucleus sampling; presence/frequency penalty reduce repetition. We'll show examples.
[04:30] Ethan: Also mention default rate limits and retry guidance \u0004 we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and an idempotency key for non-idempotent operations.

[05:00] Maya: Demo time \u0004 two requests side-by-side. First: temperature 0.0, second: temperature 0.8. Streaming both so you can see differences.
[05:22] [streaming demo noise \u0004 partial token outputs in console]
[06:00] Maya: You can see temperature 0.0 produces short, direct confirmations: \"Payment of $12.50 to Merchant X confirmed.\" Temp 0.8 returns a more verbose, sometimes chatty phrasing. For transactional messages we usually advise low temp.

[07:10] Carlos: What about retries? If we get a 429 or 503 mid-conversation, how does state and context get preserved?
[07:18] Maya: Good question. For small transient errors we recommend client retries with exponential backoff. For chat flows that maintain context, you should: 1) keep the message history on the client 2) use an idempotency token (Idempotency-Key header) per user-turn to avoid duplicate side-effects 3) if streaming failed after partial tokens, either re-start the request with the same idempotency key or resume logic if you persisted the last token \u0004 but resume is more complex.
[07:55] Priya: So there's no server-side resume yet?
[07:58] Maya: Correct, currently Redwood's hosted API doesn't support automatic resume of a partially delivered stream. We recommend safe retries and client-side reconciliation. For payments flows, treat model outputs as advisory until backend confirms.

[09:10] Maya: On rate limits \u0004 each account has per-key quotas and per-minute bursts. The Console shows token usage and per-route limits. If you hit 429s we'll return a Retry-After header, and our SDKs honor that automatically if you enable the retry middleware.
[09:35] Ethan: We also expose per-route throttles so you can pin high-priority endpoints (confirmation flows) to a higher tier. For enterprise customers we can set custom SLAs.

[10:40] Maya: Quick dive into streaming events \u0004 you'll get data: { "id":..., "delta": "text chunk" } events, and an end event. The SDK exposes an async iterator in Node and Python. Example usage in node: for await (const chunk of client.stream.create(...)) { process(chunk.delta) }
[11:05] [minor transcription glitch: 'iterator' heard as 'it a r a tor']
[11:18] Priya: For SDKs, do you buffer or emit per-token?
[11:22] Maya: We emit events as chunks; the client can batch up tokens into sentences if you prefer. There's a small default buffer to avoid extremely chatty event rates.

[12:40] Maya: Now talking about parameters \u0004 max_tokens ensures you don't overrun expected output. For very short confirmations use max_tokens=30. Also use stop sequences to ensure model stops at newline or a token like "</CONFIRM>" if you have structured output.
[13:05] Carlos: Do you recommend structured output vs free text? We need strict JSON for downstream processing.
[13:12] Maya: If you need strict JSON, use Redwood's structured output helpers or function/tool calls \u0004 or a schema-enforced response. We often use a JSON wrapper prompt + stop sequences and validate server-side. Console has examples under "Patterns -> Structured outputs".

[14:30] Liam: Quick question on cost: for streaming, are tokens billed same as non-streaming?
[14:34] Ethan: Yes, billing is per token consumed/generated regardless of streaming. But streaming may reduce client perceived latency which indirectly affects cost via prompt engineering and shorter outputs.

[15:20] Maya: Now retries deeper \u0004 recommended backoff: initial wait 100\u0004100-200ms, multiply by 2, add jitter, cap at ~5s for user-facing flows. For background batch jobs you can use longer caps. Always honor Retry-After when provided.
[15:45] Maya: For idempotency, include Idempotency-Key per high-impact request (charge intent, refund). If you retry with the same key and the server already processed the operation, the server will return the original result or a 409 depending on semantics.

[17:00] Priya: How do you surface request logs for debugging?
[17:05] Ethan: Console has per-request traces, token-level breakdown, latency histogram. For Private/Dedicated customers we expose more detailed audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM.

[18:30] Maya: Quick mention of server-side batching and KV cache \u0004 not something you as a user configure in Hosted mode, but it helps throughput. If you need predictable latency we can discuss Dedicated where you get reserved capacity.
[19:00] Carlos: We'll probably start hosted to evaluate and then maybe Dedicated for production if latency SLOs need it.

[20:10] Maya: Now a short demo on retries in SDK \u0004 I'll simulate a 503 and show automatic retry with backoff turned on.
[21:02] [demo: SDK console logs showing request id and retry attempts 1,2,3]
[21:30] Maya: You can see the SDK attaches a request-id header and we log attempts in Console. If the post-call side effect executed in your backend, you should use idempotency.

[22:50] Liam: Any hard limits on message history length? Will longer context cause timeouts?
[22:58] Maya: There are model context limits (e.g., 8k/32k tokens depending on model). For long histories we recommend summarization or context-windowing. Also note that larger inputs increase latency and token cost.

[24:10] Priya: For experiments, can you recommend temperature/top_p defaults for retrieval augmented chat?
[24:18] Maya: For RAG use low temp 0.0\u00040.3 and top_p ~0.9, because you want faithful outputs. Use re-ranking or a verification step if hallucination is a critical failure mode. Redwood Optimize can analyze your prompts and recommend quantization and batching settings as well.

[25:40] Maya: Quick console tour \u0004 API Keys, Playgrounds, per-key quotas, and the "Routes" page where you can see per-model latencies and set policies. Under "Optimize" we have recommended batching sizes and quantization profiles for cost reductions.
[26:15] [brief screenshare noise]
[27:00] Carlos: About security \u0004 we need SOC2 and KMS integration.
[27:05] Ethan: We have SOC 2 Type II; for Hosted we integrate with customer KMS for dedicated/private environments, and Private includes customer-controlled KMS/HSM. I'll attach the security whitepaper after this call.

[28:40] Priya: If we do a pilot, can you run a small benchmark against our typical payloads?
[28:45] Maya: Absolutely \u0004 we'll need your sample prompts and desired traffic profile. We'll run p50/p95 latency and token cost estimates.

[30:10] Maya: Another note on retries and streaming \u0004 if the stream disconnects mid-output and you re-issue the request, watch out for duplication; that's where the idempotency key is important and downstream dedupe. For real-time confirmation flows we often recommend: 1) generate response, 2) present to user, 3) only after user acceptance call the payment API \u0004 that reduces risk of duplicate charges.

[31:50] Liam: Do you support webhook callbacks for async generation?
[31:55] Maya: Hosted API currently supports synchronous and streaming; we also offer async job endpoints for long-running tasks which can be polled or use webhooks in some setups.

[33:10] Ethan: For SLA discussion we'll bring in our solutions engineering and customer success; Dedicated gives stronger latency guarantees and isolation.

[34:40] Maya: Let's show a sample retry policy code snippet \u0004 pseudo:
- attempt = 0
- while attempt < max_attempts:
    try request
    if success break
    else wait = base * 2**attempt + jitter
    attempt++
- if still failing escalate or surface to user

[35:20] [small interruption, background noise]
[36:05] Priya: One more question \u0004 how do you recommend handling tokenization mismatch for non-ASCII currencies?
[36:12] Maya: Models tokenize currencies fine; always include canonical currency codes and avoid abbreviations in prompts to reduce tokenization ambiguity. We can help evaluate with sample strings.

[37:30] Carlos: Ok, this is helpful. Can you summarize the recommended defaults for a payment confirmation endpoint?
[37:36] Maya: Sure \u0004 temperature: 0.0\u00040.2, max_tokens: 30, stream: true (for faster perceived latency), stop sequences: ["\\n","</CONFIRM>"], idempotency-key: yes, retry policy: exp backoff with jitter starting 100\u0004100-200ms cap 5s, honor Retry-After, validate output server-side, and consider Dedicated if p95 latency needs to be <300ms consistently.

[39:00] Ethan: I'll send the pricing and hosted vs dedicated document and our security whitepaper. Maya will run a quick latency benchmark with your sample prompts once Carlos shares them.

[40:10] Liam: Timeline \u0004 we want to decide pilot by end of month, so please send materials sooner.
[40:18] Ethan: Will do. Any blockers?
[40:22] Carlos: None immediate. We'll share prompt set and expected volumes.

[41:10] Maya: Thanks everyone, I'll follow up with a small checklist for the pilot and the benchmark instructions.
[41:18] Ethan: Thanks all, end of recording.

References shared: Hosted vs Dedicated pricing deck (link dropped in chat), Security whitepaper (will be sent), Latency benchmark spreadsheet (to be populated by Redwood SE).

End of transcript.
